primary_claim: Among three approaches to crosscoder feature ablation/steering (single-layer naive, many-layer naive, gradient-descent perturbation), the perturbation-based method is the least sensitive to hyperparameter tuning while achieving comparable quantitative performance, suppressing a sleeper-agent trigger's effect at cross-entropy close to the other methods' best settings.
stated_future_work: Investigate these approaches on a wider range of models and features/behaviours, particularly a deeper model where behaviours are more localised to particular layers
Do the single layer or many layer steering approaches but with automated hyperparameter estimation
Do the perturbation approach but add a term to the loss to penalise disrupting other features
Do the perturbation approach but instead of full gradient descent take the direction of steepest descent and use that as a steering vector
limitations_stated: The perturbation approach is quite computationally intensive, since it requires doing gradient descent to find the perturbation at every token
The perturbation approach has some risk of producing adversarial example style effects that aren't representative of the network in normal operation
In a preliminary look at steering/clamping the perturbation approach didn't give as good results as other simpler approaches
Only had time to do a brief qualitative analysis of steering/clamping
quote: For ablation, the “perturbation” approach has proved the easiest to use, since it is the least sensitive to hyperparameter tuning.
